records.title: The Oldest Migration on the Bay
records.excerpt: On a handful of nights each spring, timed to the moon, Delaware Bay hosts what wildlife agencies call the largest horseshoe crab spawning event on Earth — feeding a shorebird that flies here from the bottom of South America and cannot finish the trip without it.

records.title: The Galloping Dune
records.excerpt: Delaware's tallest sand dune buried a WWII bunker, swallowed a pine forest, and earned its nickname because it used to move. Nearby, part of the park still does.

records.title: Where the Marsh Is Going
records.excerpt: Nearly half of Delaware's wetlands lie between the tides, quietly filtering water, buffering storms, and raising nearly every fish on your plate. As seas rise, the state's plan isn't to hold the line — it's to let the marsh move.

records.title: The Towers on the Dunes
records.excerpt: Every summer thousands of people photograph the concrete towers along the Delaware coast without knowing what they are. They were optical instruments, built to last about ten years.

records.title: Why Delaware Looks Like That
records.excerpt: Delaware's northern boundary is a circular arc, unlike any other state line in the country. It exists because of a property dispute and a survey nobody could execute cleanly.
records.town: How Delaware Became Delaware · Installment 6 of 9

records.title: Three Counties Become the First State
records.excerpt: Delaware declared independence from Britain and Pennsylvania in the same week of 1776 — and eleven years later became the first state to ratify the Constitution, in a rented tavern, unanimously, in five days.
records.town: How Delaware Became Delaware · Installment 7 of 9

records.title: The Six O'Clock Shift at Indian River Inlet
records.excerpt: Every morning the surfcasters pack up right as the paddleboarders wade in — a ten-minute handoff between two different Delawares.

records.title: What the Boardwalk Smells Like in July
records.excerpt: Grotto pizza, salt water taffy and sunscreen, in that order, from the top of Rehoboth Avenue to the water.

records.title: A Field Guide to Bethany's Bandstand Nights
records.excerpt: Beach chairs go down by 7, the band starts by 8, and nobody in Bethany seems to be in a hurry to leave once it's over.

records.title: The Unmarked Trail Behind Gordons Pond
records.excerpt: Most people park at Gordons Pond, walk the boardwalk to the beach, and turn around. The trail that keeps going is where the park gets quiet.

records.title: Low Tide at Assateague Is a Different Island
records.excerpt: When the water pulls back, the horses come down off the dunes to graze flats that don't exist three hours later.

records.title: The Last Seventeen Hundred
records.excerpt: Delaware refused to abolish slavery in February 1865 — for fewer than 1,800 people, in a state where nine in ten Black Delawareans were already free. The Emancipation Proclamation never applied here, and the legislature did not ratify the Thirteenth Amendment until 1901.

records.title: In His Boots and Spurs
records.excerpt: The most famous sentence about Caesar Rodney's ride was written thirty-seven years later, by a man correcting somebody else's version of events. What the record actually supports — and why Delaware needed the story.

records.title: The Colony That Failed and Stayed
records.excerpt: New Sweden lasted seventeen years and surrendered without a shot. Almost everybody who lived there stayed for good — and by staying, made the lower Delaware a different place from the province upriver.

records.title: The Ladder off Cape Henlopen
records.excerpt: Most days and nights of the year, someone climbs a rope ladder up the side of a moving ship east of Cape Henlopen. It is how every large vessel enters Delaware Bay, and it has been happening here since 1650.

records.title: The Attic in Dover
records.excerpt: Every astronomer alive sorts stars using a system worked out by a shipbuilder's daughter from Dover. Annie Jump Cannon classified roughly 350,000 stars by eye — more than any human being who has ever lived.

records.title: The Standing Dead
records.excerpt: Bare trunks standing in open marsh along Delaware Bay look like an ending. They are the opposite: they mark the line where the marsh is climbing inland — which is the only escape route it has.

records.title: Read the Apron
records.excerpt: The most useful thing to know about crabbing in Delaware is how to turn a crab over. The shape on its belly tells you what you are holding, whether you can keep it, and whether you should.

records.title: Three Hundred Dollars
records.excerpt: In 1907 a doctor outside Wilmington needed $300 to keep a tuberculosis sanatorium open through the winter. His cousin raised ten times that by selling penny stamps that carried no mail — and accidentally founded a national institution.

records.title: The Patience of Herons
records.excerpt: A great blue heron stands four feet tall, spans six feet, and weighs about as much as a housecat. Almost everything it does is waiting — and the strike, when it comes, is one of the fastest things a large animal does.

records.title: The Refuge Loop
records.excerpt: Delaware's two national wildlife refuges are best watched from inside a car, on a falling tide, with the engine off. Everything else about Bombay Hook and Prime Hook follows from getting that right.

records.title: What the Dunes Were For
records.excerpt: The parking lot at Cape Henlopen sits on top of a gun battery. Delaware's most-visited state park is laid over a coastal fortress built to close the mouth of Delaware Bay — and the only enemy warship that ever arrived came in flying a surrender signal.

records.title: Gordon's Pond to the Water
records.excerpt: A local's turn-by-turn guide to one of the best easy walks near Rehoboth and Lewes — the boardwalk everyone takes, and the quiet trail past it that most people never find.

records.title: Lewes Canal to the Harbor
records.excerpt: Park once and walk the whole thing — historic Lewes, the canal, the free Lightship Overfalls, and the pier where the evening ferry comes in.

records.title: Surf Fishing Delaware
records.excerpt: Read the beach, choose the bait, and know the rules — a practical field guide for Cape Henlopen, Delaware Seashore, Fenwick Island and Beach Plum Island.

records.title: The Best Sunset Spots on the Coast
records.excerpt: Five real spots, one per town — the golden-hour recommendation we'd actually give a friend, not a highlight reel.

records.title: Lewes
records.excerpt: Delaware's oldest town has a beach almost as an afterthought — everything else came first.

records.title: Rehoboth Beach
records.excerpt: The boardwalk that taught half the Mid-Atlantic what a beach vacation is supposed to feel like.

records.title: Dewey Beach
records.excerpt: Ocean on one side, bay on the other, and about four blocks of sand between them.

records.title: Bethany Beach
records.excerpt: A small boardwalk, a Sunday-night bandstand, and a pace that never speeds up much past a walk.

records.title: Fenwick Island
records.excerpt: A quiet lighthouse town at Delaware's southern edge, close enough to Ocean City to borrow its energy without keeping it.

records.title: Cape Henlopen
records.excerpt: Dunes, pine forest and a WWII watchtower, all inside the point where Delaware Bay hands off to the Atlantic.

records.title: Assateague Island
records.excerpt: A barrier island with no boardwalk, no traffic light and a herd of wild horses that outrank everyone.

records.title: Ocean City
records.excerpt: Bigger, brasher and three miles longer than anything Delaware's beaches attempt — and it knows it.
